rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Reduce gradient steepness while keeping the solvent window and temperature fixed to test whether the critical pair responds to slope. The modest extension should keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

The critical pair improved with a shallower gradient, so reduce the slope further while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. This should preserve early-peak separation and may achieve full resolution with the last peak still within 10 minutes.

Injection 3 achieved the maximum CRF; now raise temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect on the critical pair, which has only a small resolution margin.

Return to the temperature that achieved full resolution and raise phi0 one grid step to shorten retention while making the gradient slightly shallower. The early pair has substantial separation margin, so this tests a faster method without the adverse temperature-selectivity shift.

Test whether a larger temperature increase carries the critical pair through its selectivity crossover and restores separation in reversed order while shortening retention. Keep the gradient fixed to interpret the temperature response, retaining injection 3 as the maximum-score fallback.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 55 C to improve the newly limiting pair while checking that the other close pair remains resolved. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially matching the maximum CRF with a shorter separation than injection 3.

Use a gradient slope between injections 6 and 7 to shorten the fully resolved separation while targeting R just above 1.5 for both critical pairs. The reduced final organic fraction remains well above the observed elution window.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek a shorter separation, with the resulting shallower slope potentially supporting the limiting middle pair. Check early-peak resolution carefully because those peaks are approaching the unretained region.

Lower phi0 to recover selectivity for the limiting middle pair and improve early retention, while using a steeper gradient to shorten the separation. This tests whether the starting-solvent benefit can compensate for the resolution loss from a faster gradient.

Extend injection 10’s gradient by one step to bring the limiting pair above R = 1.5 while monitoring the other close pair. This should retain much of its speed advantage over the fully resolved methods already found.

Choose a slope between injections 10 and 11, targeting full resolution with a shorter last-peak time than injection 11. The lower endpoint remains comfortably above the last peak’s estimated elution composition.

Increase the slope slightly relative to injection 12 to shorten the separation while targeting R just above 1.5 for both close pairs. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so all compounds should still elute during the gradient.

With a maximum-score method secured, test a cooler selectivity regime that may separate the middle cluster under a faster gradient. The stronger starting solvent and shorter gradient should help offset the increased retention at 25 C.

Test a substantially faster gradient at the highest temperature to see whether the limiting middle pair separates again after an elution-order crossover. This explores a potentially much shorter separation while retaining injection 13 as the fastest fully resolved method so far.

Shorten the gradient one step to test whether the limiting pair on this high-temperature selectivity branch improves with increasing slope. Monitor the neighboring pair closely, since its resolution margin in injection 15 was small.

Test an intermediate cooler temperature for a faster fully resolved alternative, avoiding the multiple coelutions seen at 25 C. Lowering phi0 relative to the 40 C optimum may also improve selectivity within the middle cluster.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves the limiting pair enough to permit a steeper gradient than injection 13. Monitor both middle-cluster pairs, since the second has little resolution margin at 55 C.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 18 to test the fastest fully resolved boundary at the lowest starting organic fraction. This may improve the nearly limiting pair while reducing resolution of the other close pair, so both must remain above 1.5.

Trim injection 18’s unused high-organic gradient segment while preserving its successful slope. The last peak’s estimated elution composition is about 0.57, so all peaks should remain inside the gradient and retain full resolution.

Test a lower starting organic fraction on the fast 60 C branch to measure how its critical cluster responds to the solvent window. This also improves early retention while retaining a steep gradient and a likely last-peak time near five minutes.

Probe the remaining intermediate-temperature regime with a faster gradient and strong early retention to look for a shorter fully resolved separation. Injection 18 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if this selectivity change introduces coelution.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 13 to locate the full-resolution speed boundary at phi0 = 0.10. The limiting pair may fall just below 1.5; injection 18 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Test whether a steeper gradient at 50 C improves the remaining critical cluster enough to produce a substantially faster fully resolved method. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this injection probes an alternative speed boundary without displacing the confirmed method.

Trim injection 12’s unused gradient tail while preserving its fully resolving slope and slightly larger minimum-resolution margin than the fastest confirmed method. The last peak should elute near 8.0 minutes, before the gradient ends at the outlet, preserving the maximum CRF.
